topic: Flow and value: effectiveness, efficiency, predictability

notes.front: What is an effective workflow, in The Kanban Guide?
notes.back: One that delivers what stakeholders want when they want it.
notes.explanation: It is one of three qualities the Guide asks you to balance; the next two cards give the others.
notes.example: A team that delivers the reports its users asked for, in time for the meeting they need them for.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Why Use Kanban”, p. 4

notes.front: What is an efficient workflow, in The Kanban Guide?
notes.back: One that allocates available economic resources as optimally as possible to deliver value.
notes.explanation: Effective asks “the right thing at the right time?”; efficient asks “at what use of resources?”.
notes.example: Two teams deliver the same features on time; the one that needs fewer people-hours to do it is more efficient.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Why Use Kanban”, p. 4

notes.front: What is a predictable workflow, in The Kanban Guide?
notes.back: One where you can accurately forecast value delivery within an acceptable degree of uncertainty.
notes.explanation: Predictable does not mean certain: the forecast only has to be accurate within uncertainty that is acceptable.
notes.example: A team that can say “this will most likely be done within two weeks” and is usually right.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Why Use Kanban”, p. 4

notes.front: What does value optimization mean in The Kanban Guide?
notes.back: Striving to find the right balance of effectiveness, efficiency and predictability.
notes.explanation: The Guide says most workflows exist to optimize value, and Kanban does so by optimizing flow.
notes.example: Rushing everything out may please stakeholders now but waste money and make dates unreliable; value optimization looks for the balance instead.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Why Use Kanban”, p. 4

notes.front: According to the Guide, how does Kanban set out to optimize value?
notes.explanation: Most workflows exist to optimize value, so Kanban works on flow, the movement of potential value through a system.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Why Use Kanban”, p. 4

notes.front: Value optimization is about finding the right {{c1::balance}} among effectiveness, efficiency and predictability.
notes.explanation: No one of the three is maximized at the expense of the others.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Why Use Kanban”, p. 4

notes.front: The Guide says Kanban system members should aim for a {{c1::sustainable}} balance among effectiveness, efficiency and predictability.
notes.explanation: A balance that can be kept up over time, not a short burst.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Why Use Kanban”, p. 4

notes.front: Kanban’s strategy is to get Kanban system members to ask the right questions {{c1::sooner}}, as part of a continuous improvement effort.
notes.explanation: Earlier questions mean problems with effectiveness, efficiency or predictability surface while they can still be dealt with.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Why Use Kanban”, p. 4

notes.front: What does the Guide say, ultimately, Kanban’s strategy helps you do?
notes.explanation: The Guide names this as the ultimate aim of Kanban’s strategy, after the balance of effectiveness, efficiency and predictability.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Why Use Kanban”, p. 4

notes.front: What did the December 2020 Guide say about optimization and maximization?
notes.back: “Optimization does not necessarily imply maximization.” The May 2025 text no longer includes this sentence.
notes.explanation: The idea survives in 2025 as “the right balance” of effectiveness, efficiency and predictability.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (December 2020), “Why Use Kanban?”, p. 4

notes.front: Why do the Guide’s authors prefer “optimizing” value to “maximizing” it, according to the Kanban Pocket Guide?
notes.back: Maximizing is easy short term, e.g. by burning people out, and pushing one of effectiveness, efficiency or predictability up can push the others down.
notes.explanation: Optimizing means finding the right balance within your constraints. The Pocket Guide is by Daniel Vacanti and colleagues.
notes.source: The Kanban Pocket Guide (Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, 2022), ch. 5 “Improving a Workflow to Optimize for Flow”, PDF p. 55

notes.front: A manager asks how the Guide says Kanban improves the value a team delivers. Which answer matches the Guide?
notes.choices:
A) By optimizing flow
B) By maximizing the output of each person
C) By fixing a detailed plan and sticking to it
notes.choicesExplained: B: the Guide seeks a balance of effectiveness, efficiency and predictability, not maximum output. C: the Guide asks members to keep improving their workflow, including just-in-time changes, not to stick to a fixed plan.
notes.explanation: The Guide’s strategy is to optimize value by optimizing flow.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Why Use Kanban”, p. 4

notes.front: Stakeholders keep receiving features they did not want, or too late to use. Which quality of the workflow is weak?
notes.explanation: An effective workflow delivers what stakeholders want when they want it.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Why Use Kanban”, p. 4

notes.front: A team delivers what stakeholders want, on time, but uses far more budget and people than it needed. Which quality is weak?
notes.explanation: An efficient workflow allocates available economic resources as optimally as possible to deliver value.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Why Use Kanban”, p. 4

notes.front: Nobody on a team can say, even roughly, when an item will be done. Which quality is weak?
notes.explanation: A predictable workflow can forecast value delivery accurately within an acceptable degree of uncertainty.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Why Use Kanban”, p. 4

notes.front: A team pushes for speed alone, and its costs and delivery dates become erratic. Which idea in the Guide has it lost sight of?
notes.back: Value optimization: finding the right, sustainable balance of effectiveness, efficiency and predictability.
notes.explanation: Pushing one quality hard at the expense of the others is not the balance the Guide asks for.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Why Use Kanban”, p. 4

notes.front: A team only discovers at the end of each quarter that its delivery is in trouble. What does Kanban’s strategy aim for instead?
notes.back: Asking the right questions sooner, as part of continuous improvement.
notes.explanation: The Guide’s strategy is to get members asking the right questions sooner, in pursuit of effectiveness, efficiency and predictability.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Why Use Kanban”, p. 4

notes.front: A team weighs taking on an urgent request now against keeping its other delivery forecasts reliable. Which ultimate aim of Kanban’s strategy does this concern?
notes.explanation: The choice trades effectiveness for one stakeholder against predictability for others, which is the kind of trade-off the Guide names.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Why Use Kanban”, p. 4

notes.front: What is the difference between an effective and an efficient workflow?
notes.back: Effective: delivers what stakeholders want when they want it. Efficient: uses available economic resources as optimally as possible to deliver value.
notes.explanation: A workflow can be one without the other, which is why the Guide asks for a balance.
notes.contrast: Effective is about the right thing at the right time; efficient is about the resources used.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Why Use Kanban”, p. 4
